cell16CanaryRuntimeControl.what: §7 row 16's second runtime half: the control proving the Trunk step stays observably failed while the canary job stays non-blocking.

note: This is the tuple M2b requires, and the shape matters: job-level `continue-on-error` does
NOT make the job conclude success. It stops the job's failure from failing the WORKFLOW RUN.
Revision 28 of the plan asked for step-failure with job-success, which that scope cannot
produce. The canary can never block because its context is NOT REQUIRED — not because its
job concludes green.

howTheStimulusArose: STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT DIFFERS FROM THE PLAN'S PRESCRIPTION.
M2b prescribes a provenance-bound disposable fork as the stimulus, and its stated reason is
that no lint-failing commit can otherwise reach a branch the canary watches: `push.branches` is
exactly [main, alpha], both are protected by ruleset Control with an empty bypass_actors, and
no additional in-repo branch can match.
The M2a catch-up merge falsified that assumption. Merging main into alpha (PR #86, 92 commits)
carried a PRE-EXISTING SC2250 in .githooks/pre-commit that is `new` relative to alpha's older
baseline but baseline relative to main. The commit reached alpha legitimately, through the PR
process and its five required checks, and the canary then fired on the push.
The outcome was PREDICTED BEFORE THE MERGE, not rationalised after: the same single SC2250 was
identified on PR #86's advisory trunk-check run and reported to the maintainer, who elected to
accept it rather than fix it first. So the diagnostic was known in advance and then observed.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: it is not a fork-based stimulus, and it was incidental rather
than deliberately induced. A reviewer who reads M2b's prescription as normative rather than as
one means to the end should treat M2b's runtime half as still open and run the fork exercise.
The argument for accepting it: the requirement is to CAUSE a controlled canary failure and
record the tuple bound to a lint diagnostic, and this observation is on production
infrastructure rather than a fork — the path that actually matters.
whatRemainsForM2b: If the fork-based stimulus is judged necessary, it still needs: a provenance-bound disposable
fork whose default branch is named `main`, carrying the same canary workflow at the same SHA
pins, with GitHub Actions ENABLED in that fork (they are disabled on forks by default, and
without enabling them the stimulus silently produces nothing and this half is unfalsifiable).
whyItLivesHere: It was first written to a standalone `COREDEV-2780-m2b-canary.json`, which the contract has
never heard of and nothing reads. §7's inventory and its ownership table both already assign
this observation to THIS file: `cell 16's ruleset read and its canary runtime control`, and
`the control proving the Trunk step stays observably failed while the job stays non-blocking`.
The repo has paid for that shape once already — `_recorded_remote_halves()`'s docstring
records rollout.json being named as owner in prose and parsed by nothing (codex, PR #84).
Conforming the evidence to the contract is cheaper and truer than amending the contract to
match where the evidence happened to land.

cell12DualBaseCheckRuns.what: §7 row 12's dual-base provenance-bound check runs, and the strict/advisory discrimination they carry.
why: A GREEN run cannot prove the gate is strict. With no findings, advisory and strict both
conclude success — they are indistinguishable. Only a RED run discriminates:
advisory  Trunk fails -> job failure -> WORKFLOW RUN SUCCEEDS
strict    Trunk fails -> job failure -> WORKFLOW RUN FAILS
That is why M3 requires both per base, and why revision 1 of the plan was wrong to accept a
context observed only while failures were suppressed — one that had never been able to fail.
A check run describes the JOB, so `checkRunConclusion` cannot by itself name which step
failed. M3's checklist binds the TRUNK STEP's API-reported `conclusion`, so each half below
records it as `trunkStepConclusion`, read from the workflow-jobs record.
stepScope.jobIdIsCheckRunId: That endpoint returns the job id, and on both runs below it equals the `checkRunId` already recorded (101560257395, 101560280950), so the step record is addressable from what is here with no second identifier to drift.

note: Meaningful as STRICT green only because the red observation below establishes that this
workflow version has no continue-on-error. PR #92 is branched from #91, so both ran the
same strict workflow via the pull_request merge ref.

boundDiagnostic.why: A setup, checkout or network failure would also fail the run while Trunk never reached lint evaluation. This names the linter, file, line and column, so the failure is bound to lint rather than to infrastructure.

note: THE WORKFLOW RUN CONCLUSION IS WHAT DISCRIMINATES STRICT FROM ADVISORY. Under M2's advisory
exemption this would read `success` with the job still `failure`. It reads `failure`, so the
job-scoped continue-on-error is genuinely gone.
The step conclusion is a SEPARATE requirement, not that inference: `trunk` (step 6) is the only
step that failed — steps 1-5, set-up, checkout and the three guards, all concluded `success` —
so the failure is located at lint evaluation, not upstream of it.
The PR is never merged, BY INSTRUCTION. Pre-M4 that is DISCIPLINE, not enforcement:
`trunk-check` is not one of Control's five required contexts (rollout.json records
`trunkCheckAbsentPreM4: true`), on de88d32 all five required contexts are `success` with only
`trunk-check` `failure`, and GitHub therefore reports PR #92 `mergeable: MERGEABLE`,
`mergeStateStatus: UNSTABLE` — its name for `mergeable, with a non-required check failing`.
Control's empty bypass_actors guarantees only that those five cannot be WAIVED; it cannot make
a non-rule block a merge. Its other rules, `deletion` and `non_fast_forward`, do not stop a
fast-forward push either, so no ruleset route is closed on this SHA (derived from the rules; no
push was attempted). What holds this commit off `main` is the never-merge instruction plus the
local pre-commit gate recorded below — which is itself bypassable. M4 makes this enforcement.

howTheRedCommitWasMade: The local pre-commit trunk gate BLOCKED the lint-failing commit, correctly — stopping new
findings is its purpose. Producing red-run evidence therefore requires --no-verify, which is
inherent to the observation rather than a shortcut, and is recorded here so it is not mistaken
for carelessness. The checks --no-verify skips were run by hand first: gitleaks on the staged
change (no leaks), version-sync, plugin assembly, hooks manifest.

theRoute: The red evidence comes from a PR TARGETING alpha whose head is deliberately red and is NEVER
MERGED — the check runs on the PR head, so no broken commit ever lands. Push-event red evidence
would belong to the non-required canary instead.
WHY IT IS NEVER MERGED, STATED CORRECTLY. Pre-M4 this is DISCIPLINE, not enforcement.
`trunk-check` is NOT one of Control's five required contexts (validate, py39-smoke, secret-scan,
load-check, redactor-equivalence (ubuntu-latest)), so a commit failing only `trunk-check` can
still satisfy every rule the ruleset enforces. Control's empty bypass_actors guarantees only that
those five cannot be WAIVED; it cannot make a non-rule block anything. Its other rules, `deletion`
and `non_fast_forward`, do not stop a fast-forward either. So NO ruleset route is closed on this
SHA — the same conclusion the `main` record above reaches, and this key previously contradicted.
What holds PR #97 off `alpha` is the never-merge instruction plus the local pre-commit gate, which
is itself bypassable. M4 is what turns this into enforcement.
